title: Is working from home holding you back in your career?
description:
Working from home has plenty of benefits: no commute, greater flexibility and the chance to catch up on household chores during your break. But for young people starting out their careers, could this extra freedom actually have a negative impact on career progression?

Emer Moreau, a BBC Business Reporter, breaks it down. She explains how the pandemic led to a huge increase in at-home and remote working, and looks at how many people have now returned to in-person work.

She also discusses the impact working from home has on productivity, how it affects the social nature of working life, and the ways it can slow someone's effort to climb the career ladder. We also hear from young people about their experiences with remote working.

summaryZh: 本集 BBC 節目《What in the World》探討居家辦公 WFH 是否會阻礙年輕人的職涯發展。主持人 Hannah Gelbart 與 BBC 商業記者 Emer Moreau 指出，全球目前約有 3.3 億人實施遠端或混合辦公，但統計顯示 24 歲以下的年輕員工遠端工作比例顯著較低。雖然遠端工作具備彈性與免通勤等優點，但缺乏能見度、合作效率降低及社交連結減少，可能減緩初入職場者的升遷速度。受訪的年輕專業人士表示，遠端工作需要付出額外努力紀錄績效以獲得重視，因此許多人更傾向兼顧彈性與人際互動的混合模式。 Emer 建議遠端工作者應主動溝通、維持曝光度並積極建立聯繫。此外，針對人工智慧 AI 取代職缺的焦慮， Emer 指出許多先前大量裁員並以 AI 取代基層員工的公司，已發現仍需要人類進行監督與訓練，目前正默默重新招募員工。
summaryEn: In this episode of What in the World, host Hannah Gelbart and BBC business reporter Emer Moreau examine whether working from home (WFH) negatively affects career growth, particularly for young professionals. While around 330 million people globally still work remotely, younger employees do so at much lower rates. Although remote work offers flexibility and saves commute time, it can hinder early-career progression due to lower visibility, reduced collaboration efficiency, and fewer networking opportunities. Young workers interviewed shared that remote setups require extra effort to document accomplishments and stay noticed, leading many to prefer a hybrid model. Emer advises early-career remote workers to stay proactive, communicate frequently, and maintain visibility. Finally, addressing concerns about AI replacing jobs, Emer notes that companies that replaced junior staff with AI are realizing human oversight and training are still necessary, and many are quietly rehiring.
